title: How anxiety affects the body
citation: Penninx, B. W., Pine, D. S., Holmes, E. A., & Reif, A. (2021). Anxiety disorders. Lancet (London, England), 397(10277), 914-927.
content:
How anxiety affects the body.

When the brain senses a possible threat, it activates the body's fight, flight, or freeze response. Heart rate increases, breathing becomes quicker, muscles tense, and attention narrows so you can respond rapidly if needed. These reactions are useful in genuinely dangerous situations, but when they happen frequently or without real danger, the body can remain on high alert. This is why anxiety often feels physical, with symptoms such as a racing heart, tight chest, shakiness, sweating, or an unsettled stomach.

Why does my mind keep jumping to worst case scenarios?

One of the most common features of anxiety is the tendency to imagine what could go wrong. The brain is trying to protect you by scanning ahead for possible threats. However, it often overestimates how likely those threats are and underestimates your ability to cope with them. This can create a cycle where worrying feels like preparation, even though it often leaves people feeling more anxious rather than more prepared.
